rationale: The recordings have had no artifact rejection, so short bursts like blinks, movement and muscle can dominate a Welch PSD that averages the means of its segments. Taking the median across segments instead (`average="median"`) makes the spectrum robust to those bursts. That should give a cleaner background band-power profile, especially the increased slow activity and reduced alpha seen in schizophrenia, and it should transfer better to other clinics' recordings without adding any parameters.

I'm adding one aperiodic (1/f) exponent per channel to the relative band powers. It is the log-log slope of the Welch PSD over 2–40 Hz, leaving out the 7–14 Hz alpha peak. The slope is thought to track the cortical excitation/inhibition balance, which is reported to be abnormal in schizophrenia. It also doesn't depend on amplitude scale or recording length, which should help on the external MSU and RepOD sets.

Relative band power only describes each channel's local spectrum. Schizophrenia is widely described as a dysconnectivity disorder, so I'm adding a second, connectivity view: the 1–45 Hz inter-channel correlation matrix, projected into Riemannian tangent space with the reference mean fitted on the training fold only. A separate, more strongly regularised logistic regression uses these features, and its probabilities are averaged with the existing band-power model. Correlation matrices don't depend on amplitude scale or recording length, which should help on the external MSU and RepOD sets.

Reports of schizophrenia dysconnectivity are frequency-specific: theta/delta coupling is higher and alpha/beta coupling is lower. A single 1–45 Hz correlation matrix blurs these opposite effects together. So I'm adding band-limited correlation matrices (theta 4–8, alpha 8–13, beta 13–30 Hz) alongside the broadband one. Each band gets its own tangent-space logistic regression, with the reference fitted on the training fold only, and their probabilities are averaged to form the connectivity half of the existing fusion. Like the broadband matrix, these are independent of amplitude scale and recording length.

I'm adding a delta-band (1–4 Hz) correlation matrix as a fifth frequency-specific tangent-space model in the connectivity half. Schizophrenia's best-replicated resting-state EEG abnormality is excess slow-wave activity and coupling. The theta, alpha and beta models capture band-specific dysconnectivity, but delta coupling is currently only mixed into the broadband matrix. Like the others, this feature doesn't depend on amplitude scale or recording length.

I'm switching every recording to a common average reference before computing both the band powers and the band-limited correlation matrices. With the original reference, a signal shared by all channels inflates every correlation, and that reference differs between clinics and amplifiers. Re-referencing should leave correlations that reflect real between-region coupling, and it should make the model less sensitive to the reference when applied to MSU and RepOD. The existing 1% identity shrinkage keeps the matrices strictly positive definite even though re-referencing removes one dimension of their rank; that removed direction is the same for every subject, so it shouldn't affect the comparison.

There has been no artifact rejection, so blinks, movement and muscle bursts get mixed into the correlation matrices. Blinks in particular are large and strongly shared across Fp1/Fp2/F3/F4, which inflates frontal "connectivity". This change splits each recording into 2-s epochs and drops any epoch where a channel's log-SD is far above that subject's usual level (robust z > 3, at most 30% of epochs dropped). All band-limited correlation matrices are then computed from the clean samples only. The threshold is relative to each subject, so it doesn't depend on amplitude scale or recording length, which should help on MSU and RepOD. Band powers are unchanged.

I'm adding a third late-fused model built on signal complexity: per-channel Higuchi fractal dimension and normalised permutation entropy. Each is computed on 4-s epochs of the 1–45 Hz signal and the median is taken across epochs. Altered EEG complexity is among the most-replicated resting-state findings in schizophrenia, and these features carry information about nonlinear temporal structure that neither band-power ratios nor correlation matrices capture. Both are independent of amplitude scale, and the per-epoch median makes them robust to artifacts and recording length, which should help on MSU and RepOD.

I'm adding amplitude-envelope correlation (AEC) matrices in theta, alpha and beta, computed from Hilbert envelopes of band-filtered signals. Each band gets its own tangent-space logistic model, and these join the existing band-limited correlation models in the connectivity half of the fusion. Waveform correlation only captures zero-lag phase-locked coupling, while slow co-fluctuation of band amplitude is a separate, phase-independent kind of functional connectivity that is reported to be altered in schizophrenia. Envelope correlations don't depend on amplitude scale or recording length either, which should help on MSU and RepOD.

Schizophrenia often slows the alpha rhythm, which moves power from upper alpha (10–13 Hz) into lower alpha (8–10 Hz), and it can shift power within the beta range too. One 8–13 Hz band and one 13–30 Hz band average these opposite shifts together. So this round splits them into alpha1 and alpha2, and into beta1 (13–20 Hz) and beta2 (20–30 Hz), in the log relative band-power model; everything else stays the same. Relative power doesn't depend on amplitude scale, so this should still transfer to MSU and RepOD.

Every connectivity model so far uses zero-lag correlation. Zero-lag coupling is dominated by volume conduction and the shared original reference, and re-referencing to remove that hurt in round 6. This round adds one more model to the connectivity average: debiasing-free weighted phase-lag index (wPLI) matrices in theta, alpha and beta, from 2-s Hann-windowed epochs. wPLI only measures lagged, non-zero-phase coupling, so it ignores common-reference and volume-conduction effects. That should capture the genuine inter-regional phase dysconnectivity reported in schizophrenia, and it doesn't depend on amplitude scale, reference or recording length, which should help on MSU and RepOD.

This adds EEG microstate dynamics to the band-power logistic model: coverage, mean duration, occurrence rate and explained variance for 4 microstate classes, plus the 12 transition probabilities between them. The 4 polarity-invariant template maps come from a label-free modified k-means on GFP-peak topographies, after average re-referencing and 2–20 Hz filtering; the templates are pooled across subjects. Altered microstate C/D coverage and duration is among the best-replicated resting-state findings in schizophrenia. These features describe sub-second temporal dynamics that neither band powers nor correlation matrices capture. They also don't depend on amplitude scale or recording length, which should help on MSU and RepOD. I'm appending them to the existing band-power model rather than adding a third fused model, because a third model hurt in round 8.

Microstates gave the biggest recent gain (round 12), but the features so far only describe first-order statistics: coverage, duration, occurrence and one-step transitions. Schizophrenia is reported to change the longer-range temporal organisation of the microstate sequence. So I'm adding two sequence-complexity features to the band-power + microstate model: the first-order entropy rate of the GFP-peak microstate label sequence (normalised by log K), and the normalised Lempel-Ziv complexity of that sequence, averaged over fixed 1000-peak windows. Fixed windows keep the features independent of recording length and amplitude scale, which matters for the 1-min MSU recordings.

I'm adding six amplitude-invariant microstate strength features to the band-power + microstate model. For each of the 4 classes I add its median GFP divided by the subject's overall median GFP. I also add the GFP-peak rate, which is how often the topography changes per second. Microstates gave the biggest recent gains, and schizophrenia is reported to change both how strongly each class is expressed and how fast the topography switches; the current features only describe the timing and sequence of the labels. Medians limit the influence of blink and muscle bursts, and the ratio form does not depend on amplitude scale or recording length, which matters for MSU and RepOD.

Lower individual alpha peak frequency is one of the best-replicated resting-EEG findings in schizophrenia. The current model only approximates it indirectly through the alpha1/alpha2 split. This change adds an explicit per-channel alpha centre-of-gravity frequency (7–13 Hz, from a 4-s Welch PSD) to the band-power + microstate logistic model. It is measured in Hz, so it doesn't depend on amplitude scale, reference gain or recording length, which matters for MSU and RepOD.

Microstate features have given the largest recent gains, but none of them describes long-range temporal structure. Schizophrenia is reported to disrupt the scale-free, long-range-dependent organisation of the microstate sequence. So I'm adding one Hurst exponent per microstate class: detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) of that class's one-vs-rest ±1 random walk, over fixed scales of 0.25–8 s. These go into the band-power + microstate logistic model. A DFA slope doesn't depend on amplitude scale, and the fixed 0.25–8 s scales fit inside a 1-minute recording, so the feature should also work on MSU and RepOD.

I'm adding one long-range temporal correlation (LRTC) feature per channel for the alpha (8–13 Hz) and beta (13–30 Hz) amplitude envelopes, appended to the band-power + microstate logistic model. Each is a DFA exponent of the Hilbert envelope, fitted over fixed 1–8 s scales. Weaker LRTC in alpha/beta oscillations is a reported schizophrenia finding (Nikulin et al. 2012), and it describes how amplitude evolves over seconds, which none of the current spectral, connectivity or microstate features capture. A DFA slope doesn't depend on amplitude scale, and the fixed 1–8 s scales fit inside the 1-minute MSU recordings. Round 16's DFA was on the microstate label sequence; this one is on oscillation amplitude envelopes.

I'm adding one feature per microstate class: how closely the subject's own average map for that class matches the group template. The microstate features so far only describe when and how strongly each class occurs, not what its scalp map looks like, and shifted class C/D topographies are reported in schizophrenia. Each class's map is the mean of that subject's polarity-aligned, unit-norm GFP-peak maps, and the feature is −log(1 − |spatial correlation|) with the group template. That is only 4 extra features, and it doesn't depend on amplitude scale or recording length, which matters for MSU and RepOD.

The band-power + microstate logistic model has grown from about 112 to about 167 features (16 channels × 8 spectral features, plus 39 microstate features) for about 80 training subjects. Its C=0.1 was fixed back in round 3, before those features were added, so the right amount of regularisation has probably changed. This change picks C for that model only from {0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3}, using a 5-fold inner CV on the training fold grouped by `ctx["groups_train"]` and scored by AUROC. Ties go to the stronger penalty, which should also generalise better to MSU and RepOD.

This adds Hjorth mobility and Hjorth complexity per channel to the band-power + microstate logistic model, from 1–45 Hz filtered 4-s epochs, logged and median-aggregated across epochs. Mobility is the signal's mean frequency and complexity is its spectral bandwidth, a time-domain view of the slowed, less complex EEG reported in schizophrenia that the band-sum powers and alpha frequency don't directly measure. Both don't depend on amplitude scale, and taking the median over epochs makes them robust to artifacts and recording length, which matters for MSU and RepOD.
